doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Al Schmitt's advice, broken tape machine and big-band veterans like Mel Powell
summary: Al Schmitt told him not to let them see you sweat; he recalls a broken tape machine and friends from the big bands, such as Mel Powell.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: I bet you were holding your breath, right?

You know there’s a great engineer/producer out in LA named Al Schmidt who is in his late 80s now. And I think he won a Grammy two years ago. He started out when he was a kid in New York. He’s one of the masters of all time. And he recorded in the early 60s Sam Cooke and people like that, up through Norah Jones. He’s still winning Grammys. He’s won I think 20, 22 Grammys. And Al told me one time, when I had one of those big dates, a roomful of players, one of the words of wisdom, “Just don’t let them see you sweat.” You always have to act confident. You can’t let them see that you’re nervous. I don’t care if it’s four people out there or 64 people out there, you can’t let them see you sweat. You’ve got to act confident. Even if you think oh my God. And I’ve had times © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

when there was 35 people sitting out there and the tape machine would break right before the session, and we’d have to sit there for an hour. You’re looking at your watch and they’re looking at their watches. Because they know they’re only there for three hours; maybe two sessions, six hours. And you’ve got to get it. And the tape machine broke one time and we wasted an hour while they fixed that. The studio is not going to pay for those musicians. But we had to cram into two hours what we would have done in three hours. But usually we’d get dates, string dates done, orchestra dates, we’d get three or four songs in a three hour session. And the same way with the rhythm section. We would almost always get at least three songs in a three hour session. That was just expected of you. And those guys that came out of the old Hollywood days or the old New York days, those big band players — I knew guys, there were guys that played with Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey, all these guys, that ended up in LA particularly, playing on movie dates. And of course not only were they great musicians but the stories they had, just unbelievable. A good friend of mine, I’m sure you’ve heard of the piano player and composer Mel Powell? When he was 18 years old he was hired by Benny Goodman to replace Teddy Wilson. And Mel Powell and I became great friends in the early 90s. He couldn’t play anymore. He had a degenerative nerve thing. But he said, oh that’s okay. He said, “Paul Hindemith taught me to compose here not here.” In fact it was Paul Hindemith — I bought three of his theory books when I was starting out, and that’s how I learned theory was Hindemith. That’s the name I was trying to come up with. Anyways, “Hindemith taught me to compose here not here.” So he was still composing. But if you listen to those old Goodman records with Peggy Lee and Mel Powell on piano, a phenomenal player. And he went from there, he got drafted and Glenn Miller had already gone into the army and he got every big band player, every key guy from Dorsey, Goodman, he had Mel Powell in that Army/Air Force band in Europe. It was like the cream of the big band crop, and I got to know a lot of those guys. And oh my gosh could they play. I mean, they could all play.
